v: Calgary's police have asked for three hundred and nine more officers by twenty thirty. Before council decides, we asked two questions. How well have the police performed for the resources they have had? And what does the evidence say about the request?

We compared Calgary with Edmonton, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Ottawa and Toronto, using Statistics Canada's figures, the police service's own reports and budget plan, and the City's population forecast. No single measure can rank a police service, so we looked at many.

From twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-five, crime severity in Calgary fell thirty-five percent, the largest fall of the six cities. Crime per resident fell twenty-six percent, and property crime per resident fell thirty-two percent.
Violent crime is the exception. The rate stayed about level, and because the city grew, violent incidents rose eighteen percent.

The clearest achievement is solving crime. The Calgary Police Service raised its clearance rate more than any of the six cities, from second lowest to the highest, narrowly ahead of Edmonton. That is the service's own work.

And it did this with fewer people. Calgary has the second fewest officers per resident of the six, and the fewest civilian staff. Since twenty nineteen, the population grew eighteen percent, but the number of officers grew only seven percent.

After inflation, spending per resident is about seven percent lower than in twenty twenty-one, and roughly level since twenty twenty-two. Forty-eight million dollars of next year's tax increase simply replaces fine revenue that moved to the City's own accounts.

The signs of pressure are real. Overtime has run at about twice its budget. About one in five officers was reported on leave or modified duty. Public confidence has fallen. And the response time to the most urgent calls rose from eight point two minutes to nine point five by twenty twenty-two. We could not find a published figure since.

The request adds one hundred and thirty-two million dollars a year by twenty thirty, about twelve percent more per resident. It would bring officers per resident most of the way back to the twenty twenty-one level, still below four of the five other cities. But it sets few targets the public can measure.

Would more officers mean less crime? Studies of many cities link ten percent more officers to about two to three percent less property crime, and about three percent less violent crime. These are not forecasts for Calgary. Our budget calculator lets you test the numbers yourself.

Our conclusion: strong performance, but increasing operational pressure. The evidence cannot settle whether the full request is the right size, because key measures, like response times and officers available, are not published.
Publishing them would let Calgarians judge whether the investment works. Read the full study, with every source and the calculator, at calgary insight dot c a.
